cues.text: Farming moved west with Anatolian households. They carried seed, livestock, tools, containers and the learned routines that made the parts work together.
Repeated crossings carried the complete system onto Aegean shores and into Thessaly.
Nothing more will ripen before winter. This harvest must feed the household, cover loss and preserve seed for spring.
Grain eaten in winter cannot cover later loss or return to the soil. The household's autumn decision now governs spring.
The protected seed returns to worked soil instead of the hearth.
At the Iron Gates, incoming farmers met established river communities. People and practices crossed through older routes, while river foods and local ancestry persisted unevenly.

Timber failed; the threshold, worked ground, graves and postholes remained. In some communities, fathers and sons held strongly to these inherited places, while women often arrived from neighbouring groups.
More households required more fields and herd lanes. Some clearings emptied and returned to grass and young trees; the carried system continued.
By 3300 BC, Europe had become a continent of fields, herds and long-lived settlements.
The steppe would meet fields to seize, stores to command, houses to inherit and paternal lines to reorder.
